Backup of previous version: draft.pre-snapshot-rules.md

Paper: Yang, Chatterjee, Udupi, Ramavarapu, Zhai (UIUC), "Skip the Compressor: Coding Agents Fix More Issues When They Pick Whole Files", arXiv 2610.21073 (15 Oct 2026). https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21073
Facts and connections: fact-ledger.md
Rule: one claim plus one image per beat, image right under the tweet that uses it, one-line caption, text explains and the image carries the numbers.

Tweet 1

A new paper from UIUC asks a simple question: when an AI coding assistant fixes a bug, which of your code should it get to read?

It can't read a whole project at once. So people shrink the code first. This paper found a plainer move works better: pick a few files and paste them in whole.

Tweet 2

Quick terms.

Context = the text you hand the model before it writes the fix.
Token budget = how much text fits in that context. A token is a word or piece of a word.
Compressor = a tool that deletes words a small model thinks don't matter.
Retriever = a search that grabs code chunks that look like the bug report.

Tweet 3

The setup is fair. 300 recent, real GitHub issues from 300 different projects, all Python.

Every method gets the same amount of text for each issue. The model writes one fix. The project's own tests decide if the bug is fixed.

Tweet 4

Whole files beat every compressor and every chunk search at the same budget. It held for both AI models they tried. Only a retriever trained to return whole functions came close, which points at the same lesson: keep code intact.

Tweet 5

Why compressors lose. A fix has to quote the old line exactly so the tool can find and replace it. Delete a few characters and the fix points at a line that doesn't exist. It never applies.

Their example is almost funny. The bug was a missing f in a Python f-string. The compressor deleted that exact f.

Tweet 6

Why search loses. It ranks code by how much it sounds like the bug report, not by whether it needs to change. On that same bug it filled the space with GitHub issue templates.

The left chart shows the trade: search keeps text exact but misses the right files. Compressors find the files but change the text.

Tweet 7

They also ran a clean test. Same winning files, but delete a fifth of the words in every line.

Fixes that apply, and bugs fixed, both fell. So mangled text hurts on its own, even when the files are right.

Tweet 8

Where each method loses the fix. Blue means the needed file was never shown. Orange means it was shown but a needed line was missing. Search mostly fails the first way. Compressors mostly fail the second.

Tweet 9

This isn't a lucky setting. The order holds as the budget grows or shrinks.

Tweet 10

How the file picker works. Show the model only the list of file paths. Ask it twice: which files must change? Keep the files both answers name. Paste them whole. Then allow up to 4 text searches for where things are defined or used.

It usually picks one or two files. And it needs no extra compression model running on a graphics card, so it costs less per bug.

Tweet 11

This lines up with three papers we covered. Fan et al. on harness design (the code around a model) kept long coding runs alive by swapping old tool output for a short stub. They removed whole pieces and never edited text inside them. Same rule here: cut whole lines, never words.

Compact Documentation found that once the real source file is in view, written summaries add nothing. SemNav showed finding the right file is the hard part. This paper puts both together: find the file, then show it exactly as written.

Tweet 12

Limits they say themselves. One fix attempt per bug, not a full assistant that can open more files or run tests. Python only. One benchmark. Running it a second time changes 9 to 19% of outcomes, so small gaps are shaky.

What I still can't answer: an assistant that can reopen files might recover from a squeezed view. The paper leaves that test for later.

Tweet 13

If you build AI coding assistants: spend your budget on choosing the right files, then show them exactly as written. If you must cut, cut whole lines.

Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21073
